title: Single-Snapshot Inference of Network Couplings from Universal Dynamics at Relative Equilibrium
authors: Moritz Lampert, Dominic Grün, Ingo Scholtes
abstract: Many real-world systems can be modelled as complex networks whose collective behaviour is governed by hidden interactions between nodes. Existing methods for inferring these interactions typically require controlled perturbations, time-resolved observations or multiple independent snapshots, all of which are often unavailable in practice. Here we show that class-based coupling strengths can be inferred from a single snapshot of node states when the system is observed close to a relative equilibrium. In this regime, all nodes share a common velocity, which can be absorbed into an effective class bias, transforming the inverse problem into a homogeneous linear system. The coefficients of this linear system are determined entirely by the observed local neighbourhoods and their coupling mechanism, enabling the application to arbitrary known coupling functions. We validate the approach on three different linear and nonlinear dynamical systems, recovering relative class-based couplings and, in special cases, absolute couplings. These results show that spatial heterogeneity can substitute for temporal sampling, enabling single-snapshot inference of hidden coupling strengths in networked dynamical systems.
summary: This paper presents a novel method to reconstruct unknown coupling strengths within networked dynamical systems using only one snapshot of node measurements. By assuming the system operates near a relative equilibrium state, the complex inverse problem is linearized into an algebraic system solvable via linear algebra techniques. This breakthrough shows that spatial structure alone can reveal hidden interaction parameters previously requiring time-series data.
main_problem: The core problem is inferring hidden, class-based coupling strengths within a complex network from only a single snapshot of the system's node states.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that this inference is possible if the system is observed near a relative equilibrium, allowing spatial heterogeneity to substitute for necessary temporal sampling.
method: They transform the inverse problem into a homogeneous linear system by exploiting the common velocity shared by all nodes at relative equilibrium. This allows parameter recovery using Total Least Squares.
model_or_system: The study analyzes dynamical systems on networks, including linear consensus dynamics and nonlinear models like Kuramoto oscillators. The dynamics are governed by coupling functions $f$ between classes of nodes.
key_observables: Reconstruction error (Frobenius norm) for couplings ($\| \hat{W}^* - W^* \|_F$) and the standard deviation of node velocities ($	ext{std}(\dot{\mathbf{x}})$).
important_parameters: The relative equilibrium state, class-specific biases ($b_z$), coupling function $f$, and network topology (ER, BA, SBM).
main_assumptions: The system must be observed close to a relative equilibrium ($\dot{\mathbf{x}} = k\mathbf{1}$), which linearizes the otherwise nonlinear inverse problem. The recovered parameters are only determined up to an unknown scale and additive shift.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate successful recovery of couplings using Total Least Squares on Kuramoto dynamics, show rank sufficiency across different network topologies (ER, BA, SBM), and demonstrate information loss if class biases are absent.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of prior methods requiring time-resolved data. It then introduces the relative equilibrium assumption to linearize the problem into a homogeneous system solvable via Total Least Squares. Validation is performed on multiple dynamical systems, comparing reconstruction errors across different network topologies and assessing necessary conditions like class biases.
why_interesting: The technique provides a powerful tool for analyzing complex dynamics where time-series data is unavailable, making it highly relevant for characterizing hidden interactions in physical or biological networks modeled by differential equations.
